title: Lane explains how ECB communication can move market rates even between policy meetings
summary: In a London speech on 10 November, Philip Lane sets out how ECB communication affects financial markets, firms and households, and why the institution changed the way it describes its decisions. The policy rate is observable, but the response to the next inflation reading or to a new source of risk is uncertain. By explaining what will guide a decision, the ECB can change the expected path of rates and financing conditions before an actual move. The evidence Lane reviews distinguishes several audiences and several kinds of news. A change in market yields around an announcement need not be a surprise about the rate set that day.

Charts 1 to 3 concern markets. Measures derived from the language of ECB communication broadly track hawkish and dovish phases in the deposit facility rate. The measured policy tone relates more strongly to the discussion of inflation than to activity. Lane notes that model-based classifications require validation. Chart 2 accumulates absolute movements in swap rates in narrow event windows. Communications between meetings can collectively move rates by amounts comparable to meeting announcements, especially at longer maturities. Adding absolute changes measures the amount of repricing, not its net direction. Chart 3 distinguishes a surprise about the current rate, a revision to the expected path, and news about market or sovereign risk. For a bondholder, each can produce a yield move with a different implication for hedging.

A meeting can also reveal how the central bank assesses the economy or how it responds to public data. A rate rise interpreted as evidence of stronger demand differs from one interpreted as an unexpected tightening given unchanged fundamentals. Lane reports that equity movements in the six weeks before a meeting help explain some measured announcement surprises, a relationship not found for speeches. Chart 6 compares estimated macroeconomic responses: communication shocks can influence activity and inflation, but generally with smaller and slower effects than surprise rate changes. These are estimates that depend on how the different shocks are identified.

Consumers encounter a different information channel. Only about one in ten had heard about the new inflation target in the months following the 2021 review. Television, radio and newspapers reached more of them than direct ECB communications. Attention to inflation rises when inflation is high, as does firms' attention in Chart 5, but familiar information may then change beliefs less. Explaining the link to borrowing costs can matter more to households than restating a target. For firms, expectations feed into price-setting, pay and investment. Neither group can be assumed to update as quickly as a rates desk following a press conference.

Lane traces the evolution from explaining decisions before the financial crisis to explicit rate guidance from July 2013 when rates were near their effective lower bound. The 2021 guidance reinforced the commitment to the symmetric 2% target during a period of persistently low inflation. The later inflation surge called for a different approach. In March 2023 the Council shifted towards explaining three criteria: incoming information about the inflation outlook, underlying inflation and the strength of transmission. Rates still rose at the next four meetings. Stating a framework therefore did not require advance commitment to the particular path that followed.

Chart 8 finds greater sensitivity of expected rates to data surprises under framework guidance than during explicit forward guidance. The lower bound, the degree of uncertainty and the economy also changed, so the chart cannot isolate the effect of wording. Lane favours retaining baseline projections as an anchor and using alternative scenarios to clarify material risks. His qualification is that published scenarios illustrate only some possible outcomes. Reading them alongside the full risk assessment is essential when assessing how an unexpected development might change the policy response.

questions.question: How much of a meeting-day move belongs to the rate path rather than to new information about growth or risk?
questions.detail: Compare intraday swap rates across maturities with sovereign spreads and equities around the decision and press conference. Apply the event classifications underlying Charts 2 and 3, then compare with intermeeting speeches. Doing so would test whether a duration hedge addresses the main exposure or leaves a material sovereign or equity risk unhedged.

questions.question: Did framework guidance itself increase the market response to inflation surprises?
questions.detail: Match releases with similar forecast errors, uncertainty and distance from the lower bound across guidance regimes, and compare one-, two- and ten-year swap responses. Use the announcement and macroeconomic surprise series underlying Chart 8. Persistence after these controls would give rates investors stronger grounds to adjust exposure around data releases instead of assuming that today's reaction reflects only changed economic conditions.

questions.question: Which channels change household or firm decisions after the message reaches them?
questions.detail: Separate knowledge of the target from revisions to expected inflation, borrowing costs, spending and pricing. Compare responses by initial attention and by exposure to traditional media or direct ECB communication. Consumer Expectations Survey modules and firm surveys could test whether a message that promptly reprices swaps also changes real decisions within the horizon assumed in a portfolio scenario.
